source.text: Source: BLS Average Price Data (APU series) • Median usual weekly earnings (BLS LEU)

scenes.voiceover: Your bag of chips is smaller. Your coffee can lost a third of its weight. Everyone says groceries are more expensive. <break time="500ms"/> But when you measure the actual price per unit against median wages... four out of six common grocery products cost LESS of your paycheck today than they did in the year two thousand.

visual.description: Visual-first hook — chips bag + coffee can shrink animations (0-5s), title fade-in at 5s, then 6 product icons at starting line, RUPI = 1.0.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="1000ms"/> The data says you're winning. <break time="500ms"/> So why doesn't it feel that way?

visual.description: Contrarian reveal — quick preview flash of final chart state (4 below, 2 above), then question text.

scenes.voiceover: Imagine you earned five hundred seventy-two dollars a week in two thousand. A dozen eggs cost ninety-one cents. Today you earn twelve hundred — but eggs cost four twenty-five. Did eggs get more expensive... or did your paycheck grow faster? <break time="500ms"/> That's the question behind what we call the Real Unit Price Index — RUPI. Take twenty-five years of Bureau of Labor Statistics prices — per pound, per gallon, per dozen — and divide each product's price growth by median wage growth.

visual.description: Split comparison card (2000 vs 2025 wages+eggs), then RUPI formula build animation.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> One means a product costs the same share of your paycheck as in two thousand. Above one — it's taking a bigger bite. Below one — wages won.

visual.description: RUPI baseline reference diagram — red zone above 1.0, green zone below, baseline at center.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Now — a common objection. If companies are shrinking packages, doesn't that hide inflation? Actually, the BLS already accounts for this. When your coffee can shrinks from sixteen ounces to ten at the same sticker price, BLS records that as a price INCREASE per pound. Shrinkflation is already baked into the numbers you're about to see.

visual.description: Coffee can shrinks animation while price tag stays fixed, per-pound counter ticks upward.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Six products. All starting at one point zero. <break time="1000ms"/> Let the race begin.

visual.description: Race chart starting position — 6 dots at RUPI 1.0, glow pulse on 'Let the race begin.'

scenes.voiceover: Two thousand to two thousand nine. <break time="500ms"/> Right away, eggs break from the pack. An avian flu scare in two thousand three pushes them up. By two thousand four, they're already about thirty percent above the baseline — more of your paycheck for the same dozen. Then a global commodity surge in two thousand seven and eight drives them higher. By two thousand eight, eggs are the clear outlier — nearly seventy-five percent more of your weekly wage than they cost in two thousand.

visual.description: Race chart animates 2000–2009. Eggs spike to ~1.73 by 2008. Chapter marker: ACT 1. How-to-read overlay.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Coffee does the opposite. It drifts steadily downward through the early two thousands. By two thousand four, a pound of ground roast takes about a quarter less of your paycheck than it did at the start of the decade. Coffee kept getting cheaper.

visual.description: Coffee line highlighted drifting to ~0.74 by 2004. Eggs dimmed.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Chips, milk, peanut butter, ice cream — they all hover near the baseline. Wages are roughly keeping pace. Nothing dramatic. Nothing alarming. <break time="500ms"/> Then two thousand eight — the financial crisis. Milk and chips push briefly above one as commodity prices surge, but by two thousand nine, most products settle back down.

visual.description: Middle 4 products near baseline. Financial crisis event marker at 2008. Brief surge, then settle.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> And behind the scenes — something quieter is happening. Häagen-Dazs shrinks its container from sixteen to fourteen ounces. Skippy redesigns its peanut butter jar — same height, deeper indent in the bottom — dropping from eighteen to sixteen point three ounces. <break time="500ms"/> Why? Because three ninety-nine is a magic number. Consumers notice when a price crosses four dollars. They don't notice when two ounces disappear. The BLS tracks price per unit, so the shrinkage shows up in the data. But the sticker price at the register? That barely moved.

visual.description: Shrinkflation annotations on paused chart: Häagen-Dazs 16→14oz, Skippy 18→16.3oz. $3.99 price tag.

scenes.voiceover: The twenty-tens. The quiet decade. <break time="500ms"/> Coffee spikes above one in twenty eleven and twelve — a global commodity boom — then falls back below. It would stay below one for years. Eggs remain volatile. The twenty fifteen avian flu outbreak pushes them nearly twice as expensive as the baseline — then they crash back down by twenty seventeen.

visual.description: Race chart continues 2010–2019. Coffee spikes 2011-12. Eggs peak 2015 (~1.93). Chapter: ACT 2.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> But look at the rest of the field. They're drifting down. Slowly. Steadily. No single dramatic moment — just a gradual slide. Peanut butter. Milk. Chips. Ice cream. All sinking below one. Wages growing just a little faster than these prices, year after year.

visual.description: Bottom 4 products drifting below baseline with green zone glow. Eggs/coffee dimmed.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Why? The post-recovery economy. Unemployment fell. Labor markets tightened, especially after twenty sixteen. Wages started climbing — not dramatically, but persistently. And food commodity prices stayed relatively flat. <break time="500ms"/> By twenty nineteen, every product sits below the baseline — most of them well below it. The chart says things are getting better. It looks like the story has a happy ending. <break time="1000ms"/>

visual.description: 2019 freeze — all 6 below 1.0. 'False happy ending' vignette with annotation.

scenes.voiceover: Except — look at the shelf, not the chart. On the chart, chips sit just below the line — barely cheaper per ounce. But on the shelf, a standard Doritos bag reportedly shrank from twelve ounces to nine and a quarter. Twenty-three percent less product. Folgers, according to consumer tracking, went from a full one-pound can to ten point three ounces — thirty-six percent less coffee in the same-looking can. <break time="500ms"/> According to the BLS, the snack food category alone saw a cumulative two point six four percent price impact from downsizing between twenty fifteen and twenty nineteen. The price per ounce held steady. The package just got smaller. <break time="500ms"/>

visual.description: PATTERN INTERRUPT — full-screen before/after split cards. Doritos 12→9.25oz (-23%), Folgers 16→10.3oz (-36%). No race chart on screen.

scenes.voiceover: And there's one more thing the data can't capture. Skimpflation. Same package, same size, same price — but cheaper ingredients. Thinner chips. Waterier ice cream. Less cocoa in the chocolate. Unlike shrinkflation, there's no government data series for this. No BLS measurement. It's real — economists acknowledge it — but it lives in the gap between what statistics can track and what your taste buds notice. <break time="500ms"/> If you were shopping during this decade, it probably didn't FEEL like things were getting cheaper. And in one sense, they weren't — per trip to the store. You were buying the same number of packages, paying roughly the same at checkout, getting less in the bag each time, and sometimes getting a lesser product too. The per-unit math works out. The grocery receipt doesn't care about per-unit math. <break time="1000ms"/> The lines are drifting down. Everything looks calm.

visual.description: Phase 1: Skimpflation concept (identical packages, degrading quality). Phase 2: Return to chart. Phase 3: Ominous still.

scenes.voiceover: Twenty twenty. <break time="500ms"/> A dip across the board. Every product appears to get cheaper overnight. But this isn't because food prices dropped. During COVID, lower-wage workers disproportionately lost their jobs — retail, hospitality, food service. The people who remained employed skewed higher-income. So the median wage jumped. Not because anyone got a raise. Because the composition of who was still working changed. <break time="500ms"/> The prices on the chart were real. The wage improvement was a statistical artifact.

visual.description: 2020 COVID dip — all lines drop. Annotation card: 'COVID Wage Anomaly.' Chapter: ACT 3.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> By twenty twenty-one, workers return — and the median normalizes. Then twenty twenty-two. Inflation surges. Supply chains still broken. Energy costs cascading through every product. Eggs spike — avian flu again, this time the worst outbreak in American history. Tens of millions of birds culled. <break time="500ms"/> Everything on the chart rises. For the first time in years, the lines are moving UP.

visual.description: 2021-2022 surge. All lines rise urgently. Eggs spike to ~1.71. Event marker: inflation + avian flu.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Twenty twenty-three and twenty-four — most products stabilize or edge back down. But not eggs. Avian flu keeps returning. And by twenty twenty-five, eggs have more than doubled relative to the baseline. More than doubled. The chart shows you exactly how far. This isn't about shrinkflation or corporate strategy — it's biology. Disease. The egg market runs on chickens, and the chickens keep getting sick. <break time="500ms"/> Coffee crosses back above one in twenty twenty-five — the first time in over a decade. Drought in Brazil. Crop failures in Vietnam. A pound of coffee now takes a bigger slice of your paycheck than it did twenty-five years ago.

visual.description: Eggs climb to 2.21× with counter. Coffee crosses 1.0. Annotations: avian flu, Brazil drought.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="1000ms"/> But when the chart freezes at twenty twenty-five... look at the full picture. Peanut butter — down more than a third from the baseline. The biggest winner for your wallet. Milk and ice cream — both well below one. Even chips, despite all the shrinkage, sit just below the line. <break time="500ms"/> Four out of six products. Cheaper relative to wages. After twenty-five years. After everything.

visual.description: Chart freezes at 2025. All 6 final RUPI values labeled. Tally: '4 of 6: Cheaper relative to wages.'

scenes.voiceover: Four out of six products, cheaper relative to wages. <break time="1000ms"/> But cheaper... for whom? <break time="1000ms"/> That index used median wages — the middle of the income distribution. The typical worker. What if we change the ruler?

visual.description: Chart dims. 'But cheaper… for whom?' large center text. Then: 'What if we change the ruler?'

scenes.voiceover: <break time="1200ms"/> Switch to the Consumer Price Index — CPI. This is the government's standard measure of inflation. It tracks roughly eighty thousand prices across the economy every month. When we use CPI instead of wages, we're asking a simpler question: did food prices outpace general inflation? <break time="500ms"/> The lines shift up. Chips crosses above one. Coffee jumps higher. Eggs climb further. Now three products cost more in inflation-adjusted terms than they did twenty-five years ago. <break time="500ms"/> Why the difference? Because median wages grew faster than inflation over this period — about a hundred and eleven percent versus eighty-seven percent. The median worker gained real purchasing power. That's a good thing. But it means the wage-deflated view is the OPTIMISTIC one.

visual.description: CPI lens switch — lines morph upward. Chips crosses 1.0. Tally: '3 of 6: More expensive.' Stat: +111% vs +87%.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="1200ms"/> Now switch to the federal minimum wage. <break time="1000ms"/> Seven dollars and twenty-five cents an hour. That's the federal minimum wage in the United States. It was set in July of two thousand nine. <break time="500ms"/> It hasn't changed since. Not once. Sixteen years. Through a pandemic. Through the worst inflation in forty years. Through everything. <break time="500ms"/> Roughly one point one million American workers earn exactly this amount. <break time="500ms"/> Millions more earn close to it.

visual.description: Min wage prelude — $7.25/hr counter dominates screen. Running ticker: '16 years, 8 months and counting.'

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Watch the lines. <break time="1000ms"/> Five of six products jump above one. The chart transforms. What looked like a story about affordability becomes a very different story. <break time="500ms"/> Eggs — a minimum wage worker now needs more than three times the work hours to buy a dozen compared to two thousand. Think about that concretely. In two thousand, a dozen eggs at ninety-one cents cost a minimum wage worker about eleven minutes of work. Today, at four twenty-five, it costs over thirty-five minutes. Same dozen eggs. Same job. Three times the effort.

visual.description: Min wage reveal — lines JUMP. 5 of 6 above 1.0. Then: 11 min vs 35 min work comparison card for eggs.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="500ms"/> Coffee. Chips. Milk. Ice cream. All above the line. Products that looked like bargains under median wages are now MORE expensive for anyone stuck at the federal floor. <break time="500ms"/> Only peanut butter stays below — barely. Just under one. The last holdout. <break time="1200ms"/> The median worker gained purchasing power over twenty-five years. The minimum wage worker lost it. Same economy. Same products. Same quarter century. A completely different experience depending on where you sit in the income distribution.

visual.description: Min wage conclusion — all products labeled. PB 'Last holdout.' Split summary: median vs min wage worker.

scenes.voiceover: <break time="1200ms"/> And one more lens. Gold. <break time="500ms"/> If you'd measured your groceries against gold's twelve-fold rise over this period... everything collapses toward zero. Eggs, coffee, chips — all on sale. Deep, deep on sale. <break time="500ms"/> But no one buys eggs with gold.

visual.description: Gold lens — all lines collapse to near zero. 0 of 6 above. Brief, philosophical.

scenes.voiceover: Same six products. Same twenty-five years. Same Bureau of Labor Statistics data. <break time="500ms"/> Under median wages — four out of six got cheaper. Under CPI — three got more expensive. Under the minimum wage — five out of six. Under gold — everything's a bargain. <break time="1000ms"/> Shrinkflation is real. Your chip bag lost twenty-three percent of its weight. Your coffee can lost more than a third. But the biggest shrinkage isn't in the package. <break time="1000ms"/>

visual.description: 2×2 grouped bar summary — products above/below 1.0 per deflator (Wage/CPI/MinWage/Gold).

scenes.voiceover: It's in the question we forgot to ask. <break time="500ms"/> Cheaper for whom? <break time="500ms"/> Same data. Same math. Different ruler. <break time="500ms"/> Different reality.

visual.description: 'Cheaper for whom?' → 'Same data. Same math. Different ruler. Different reality.' + channel logo + subscribe.
